To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

females consuming lower red meat intake diets are more likely to consume diets with lower micronutrient intake, particularly zinc and vitamin D, and are more likely to have a lower habitual dietary vitamin D intake.
Females consuming diets low in red meat (i.e. <40g/day) appear to be at increased risk of having lower intakes of zinc, iron, and vitamin B12.

females consuming less than 4 0 g total red meat per day were more likely to consume diets low in zinc, iron, potassium and vitamin B12, and had lower habitual intakes of vitamin D, than females who consumed more than 40 g red meat daily.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the nutritional impact of reducing red meat intakes for UK females.
the micronutrient intake and status of UK females consuming diets lower in total red meat.
the impact of reducing red meat intake on the micronutrients status of British females.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

red meat consumption is not a major source of micronutrients for British women and therefore blanket advice to reduce red meat consumption could have negative implications for the micronutrient status of women in the UK.
red meat intakes in the UK are associated with a higher intake of key micronutrients.
red meat intakes should be maintained at the current level, or higher, to ensure adequate intakes of micronutrients, especially for females.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
red meat is a good source of micronutrients.
blanket advice to reduce red meat intake in the UK population should be reconsidered as it could have negative impacts on the micronutrients status of the UK population.
the consumption of less than 40g of red meat daily may have a negative impact on the nutritional adequacy of the diets of women in the UK.
The main takeaway from our work is that
blanket health messages to lower total red meat intakes may have adverse implications for women's micronutrients intakes.
there is a need for a more targeted approach to dietary advice for the UK population, which considers the micronutrient needs of different groups.
blanket health messages to reduce red meat consumption may not be appropriate for women in the UK as it could have adverse implications for their micronutrient status.
